column3: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, teaches in the kingdoms of the Ganges plain; monks and nuns form the Sangha, supported by lay followers among merchants and kings.
The Mauryan emperor Ashoka turns to the Buddha's teaching, sets up edicts across his empire and, by tradition, sends missions to Sri Lanka and the north-west.
The Pali Canon is written down in Sri Lanka; in Gandhara, under Indo-Greek and then Kushan kings, Buddhist art and learning flourish.
Monks and merchants carry the teaching over the Pamirs, along the Silk Road to the oases of the Tarim basin and into China.
Mahayana sutras spread; translators such as An Shigao and Lokaksema render them into Chinese at Luoyang.
Buddhism reaches Korea (372) and wins rulers and people across north and south China.
Kumarajiva of Kucha translates the great sutras at Chang'an; Nalanda grows into a monastic university; Theravada reaches the Pyu and Mon cities of Burma.
Buddhism is brought to Japan from Baekje (538 or 552); the giant Buddhas of Bamiyan are carved.
Xuanzang returns from India to the Tang capital Chang'an (645); Yijing studies in Srivijaya; the first temples rise in Tibet.
The Pala kings of Bengal and the Sailendras of Java are great patrons: Borobudur is built; in Tibet, Samye is consecrated (around 779).
The Tang emperor Wuzong closes thousands of monasteries (845); the schools of Chan and Pure Land recover best.
Khotan falls to the Muslim Kara-Khanids (around 1006); in Burma, Anawrahta's Bagan becomes a Theravada kingdom (from 1044).
Polonnaruwa in Sri Lanka and Bagan are great Theravada capitals; in Cambodia, Jayavarman VII builds Buddhist temples such as the Bayon.
The great monasteries of Bihar and Bengal are sacked around 1200 and Buddhism fades from most of India; Theravada spreads through Burma, the Thai kingdoms and Cambodia.
Theravada is the faith of Sukhothai, Ayutthaya and the new Lao kingdom of Lan Xang; in Korea the Joseon kings (from 1392) favour Confucianism.
Islam spreads in the Malay world and Java; Turfan's Uyghurs, the last Buddhists of the Tarim basin, become Muslims.
The Mongol ruler Altan Khan gives the Tibetan lama Sonam Gyatso the title of Dalai Lama (1578), and Mongolia turns to Tibetan Buddhism.
The fifth Dalai Lama becomes ruler of Tibet (1642); in Japan every household must register with a Buddhist temple; the Kalmyks bring their faith to the Volga.
Russia recognises the Buddhist clergy of the Buryats (1741); Buddhism remains the faith of the kingdoms of Burma, Siam, Laos and Cambodia.
The Maha Bodhi Society (1891) works to restore Bodh Gaya; Japanese settlers bring Buddhism to Hawaii and California.
Buddhism suffers under communist rule in China, Tibet, Mongolia and Cambodia and spreads to the West; in 1956 B. R. Ambedkar leads hundreds of thousands into Buddhism at Nagpur.
Several hundred million Buddhists: estimates range from about 320 to 500 million, most of them in East and Southeast Asia.

column3: The hymns of the Rigveda, in an early form of Sanskrit, are composed in the Punjab for rites of fire and sacrifice to gods such as Indra, Agni and Varuna.
The Vedic tradition moves east to the Kuru and Panchala lands, where the later Vedas and the rules of sacrifice take shape.
In the kingdoms of the Ganges plain the earliest Upanishads ask about the self (atman) and ultimate reality (Brahman).
The epics, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, begin to take shape; the Buddha and Mahavira challenge the sacrifices of the Brahmins.
Brahmin traditions reach the Deccan and the far south, beside Buddhism and Jainism; the Bhagavad Gita takes shape.
Under the Gupta kings, temples, the Puranas and devotion to Vishnu and Shiva flourish; Brahmins and traders carry the gods across the Bay of Bengal.
In the south the Tamil poet-saints, the Alvars and Nayanars, sing of devotion (bhakti) to Vishnu and Shiva.
Shankara teaches Advaita Vedanta, the non-dual reading of the Upanishads; the Kailasa temple is carved at Ellora.
Hindu and Buddhist kings rule Java, Cambodia and Champa; the Shiva temple of Prambanan is consecrated in 856.
The Chola kings build great temples and carry their power to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia; raids from Ghazni strike the temples of the north-west.
Angkor Wat is built for Vishnu, the Jagannath temple of Puri rises, and Ramanuja teaches a devotional Vedanta.
Sultans rule from Delhi, while most people of the subcontinent remain Hindu; in Cambodia Theravada Buddhism replaces the Hindu court cults.
Vijayanagara, founded in 1336, becomes the great Hindu kingdom of the south; in Java, Majapahit is at its height.
Dai Viet takes Champa's capital (1471); Islam spreads in Java and Majapahit declines, while Bali keeps the old religion.
Devotional poets write in the languages people speak: Tulsidas retells the Ramayana in Awadhi (begun in 1574); Majapahit has fallen.
Temple building continues under Rajput and Nayaka rulers, and Madurai's great temple takes its present form.
The East India Company comes to rule much of India; the Bhagavad Gita is translated into English (1785).

Reformers rethink Hindu practice (the Brahmo Samaj, 1828; the Arya Samaj, 1875); indentured labourers take their faith to Mauritius, the Caribbean, Natal and Fiji; Vivekananda speaks in Chicago (1893).
The partition of 1947 divides India and Pakistan; India's constitution (1950) abolishes untouchability; Hindu communities grow in Britain, North America and the Gulf.
About 1.2 billion Hindus (2020), most of them in India and Nepal.

column3: By Jain tradition Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara after Parshvanatha, teaches non-violence and the path to liberation in the Ganges plain.
By Digambara tradition, in a famine Bhadrabahu leads monks south to Karnataka, joined by Chandragupta Maurya.
King Kharavela of Kalinga honours the Jinas in his Hathigumpha inscription; Mathura becomes a great Jain centre.
The community divides into the Digambara ("sky-clad") and Svetambara ("white-clad") traditions.
A council at Valabhi writes down the Svetambara canon (453 or 466); Jain kings and merchants flourish in Karnataka and the Tamil country.
Shaiva and Vaishnava poet-saints win many Tamil rulers away from the Jains; in Karnataka the Ganga and Rashtrakuta kings remain patrons.
The great statue of Bahubali is carved at Shravanabelagola (around 983); the marble temples of Mount Abu follow (from 1031).
King Kumarapala of Gujarat embraces Jainism under the teacher Hemachandra; in Karnataka the Hoysala kings turn to Vishnu and the Lingayat movement rises.
Jain merchants and ministers build great temples, such as Ranakpur in Rajasthan, while the Lonka movement rejects the worship of images.
Acharya Bhikshu founds the Terapanth (1760), a reformed order of the Svetambaras.
Jain merchants settle in East Africa; Virchand Gandhi speaks for Jainism at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago (1893).
Many East African Jains move to Britain in the 1960s and 1970s; communities grow in North America.
About 4.5 million Jains in India (2011 census), with communities in Britain, North America and East Africa.

column3: Guru Nanak, born in 1469, begins his mission after an experience at the river Bein (around 1499) and travels widely, teaching devotion to the one God.
Guru Nanak settles at Kartarpur (he dies in 1539); the community grows under the Gurus who follow him, and Guru Ram Das founds Amritsar (1577).

Guru Gobind Singh dies at Nanded (1708), naming the scripture the Guru; Sikh bands fight Mughal and Afghan armies, and in 1799 Ranjit Singh takes Lahore.
Ranjit Singh rules the Sikh Empire as maharaja (1801–1839); the British annex the Punjab (1849), and many Sikhs serve in their army and settle abroad.

The partition of 1947 divides the Punjab, and Sikhs leave the west for India; in 1984 the army's assault on the Golden Temple and the violence after Indira Gandhi's assassination; communities grow in Britain, Canada and the United States.
About 25 to 30 million Sikhs, most of them in the Punjab, with large communities in Britain, Canada and the United States.

column3: Zarathustra composes the Gathas in eastern Iran or Central Asia, praising Ahura Mazda, the Wise Lord; his date is disputed, and many scholars place him between about 1500 and 1000 BCE.
The worship of Ahura Mazda spreads west across the Iranian plateau among the Medes and Persians.
Darius I credits his victories to Ahura Mazda (Behistun, around 520 BCE); the Persian Empire reaches from Anatolia to the Indus.
Alexander conquers the Persian Empire (330 BCE); under Seleucid and then Parthian rule the old faith continues across Iran.
Ardashir I founds the Sasanian Empire (224) and Zoroastrianism becomes the religion of the state; the high priest Kartir organises its fire temples.
The Sasanian kings honour three great fires and try to bring Christian Armenia back to the faith (451); Sogdian merchants carry their fire temples along the Silk Road.
The Arab conquest ends the Sasanian Empire (Yazdegerd III is killed in 651); over the next centuries most Iranians become Muslims.
Priests compile the Pahlavi books (the Denkard, the Bundahishn); by the Story of Sanjan, a group of Zoroastrians settles in Gujarat, the origin of the Parsis.
Zoroastrians become a small minority in Iran, living mainly around Yazd and Kerman; the Parsis keep their faith in Gujarat.
The Iranshah fire is installed at Udvada (1742); Parsis thrive as merchants and shipbuilders in Bombay.
Parsis lead in Indian commerce and public life: Dadabhai Naoroji becomes the first Asian elected to the British House of Commons (1892).
Parsis and Iranian Zoroastrians settle in Britain, North America and Australia.
Perhaps 100,000 to 200,000 Zoroastrians, mainly in India, Iran and the diaspora.

column3: By the biblical account David makes Jerusalem his capital and Solomon builds the First Temple; the kingdoms of Israel and Judah take shape.
Assyria destroys the northern kingdom of Israel (around 722 BCE); Judah survives, and its prophets and scribes shape the books of the Bible.
The Babylonians destroy Jerusalem and the First Temple (586 BCE) and take many Judeans into exile; under Persian rule many return, and the Second Temple is completed (516 BCE).
After Alexander's conquests Jews settle across the Hellenistic world; in Alexandria the Bible is translated into Greek.
The Maccabean revolt rededicates the Temple (164 BCE); the Hasmonean kings rule Judea until Rome takes control (63 BCE).
The Romans destroy Jerusalem and the Second Temple (70) and later crush the Bar Kokhba revolt (132–135); rabbis rebuild Jewish life around the study of the law.
Judah ha-Nasi compiles the Mishnah (around 200); Jews live across the Roman and Persian empires, from Spain to Babylonia.
The kings of Himyar in Yemen adopt Judaism; under the Christian Roman emperors Jews face growing restrictions.
The Babylonian Talmud reaches its final form (around 600); Islam arises in Arabia, and most Jews come to live under Muslim rule.
The rulers of the Khazars on the Volga adopt Judaism, by most accounts in the 8th or 9th century.
Jewish life flourishes under the caliphs in Babylonia, Egypt and Spain, and in the Rhineland towns of Ashkenaz.
Crusaders massacre Jewish communities of the Rhineland (1096); Rashi teaches at Troyes.
Maimonides, born in Córdoba in 1138, writes his works in Egypt; in Kaifeng, Jews build a synagogue (1163).
England expels its Jews (1290) and France soon after; many move east, where Polish rulers invite Jewish settlers.
The Black Death brings massacres of Jews in German towns; Poland and Lithuania become new centres.
Spain expels its Jews (1492) and Portugal forces them to convert (1497); many find refuge in the Ottoman Empire and North Africa.
Joseph Karo's code of law, the Shulchan Aruch, is printed (1565); Isaac Luria teaches Kabbalah at Safed; Jews settle in Amsterdam.
Jews from Recife found the first community in New Amsterdam (1654); England readmits Jews (1656); in Eastern Europe the Cossack uprising (1648) kills many thousands.
The Baal Shem Tov's Hasidism spreads in Eastern Europe; the Haskalah, the Jewish Enlightenment, begins in Berlin.
Emancipation in Western Europe; from 1881 pogroms drive millions of Jews from the Russian Empire to America; Zionism seeks a Jewish homeland.
The Holocaust murders about six million Jews (1941–1945); the State of Israel is founded (1948), and most Jews of the Middle East and North Africa move there.
About 15 million Jews, most of them in Israel and the United States.

Many Bonpos are executed in the Dzungar invasion of Tibet (1717); New Bon treasures are still revealed in eastern Tibet.
Bon flourishes in eastern Tibet under lamas such as Shardza Tashi Gyaltsen; the canon is carved on woodblocks at Trochu.
China invades Tibet (1950), where there are about 300 Bon monasteries; Bon suffers in the Cultural Revolution, and in exile it is recognised by the Central Tibetan Administration (1979).
Scholars estimate about 400,000 Bonpos on the Tibetan Plateau (2019); Bon monasteries in Tibet have been rebuilt since 1980.

column3: The ancestors are the most honoured members of the family, and divination develops in China by 1250-1150 BCE; the worship of Shangdi is rooted in the Shang tradition.
The Yijing and the Eight Trigrams are well established; under the Zhou, Tian becomes a more abstract and impersonal idea of God.

Yin and yang and the five phases develop by the third century BCE; under the Han dynasty (from 202 BCE) people worship in she, local communities gathered at the altar of an earth god or a deified virtuous person.
From the 3rd century, with Buddhism, influences from the Indian subcontinent enter Chinese religion: processions of gods' images on carts and floats, with music and chanting.
A cult of Ganesha, the Elephant-Head God, is attested in 531.
By the Song dynasty (960-1279) folk practices blend with Buddhist, Confucian and Taoist teachings into the popular religion that lasts to the present day.
In the 14th century the Hongwu Emperor of the Ming strengthens and systematises the indigenous cults, which he calls Shendao.
The Sanyi teaching is founded in the Putian region of Fujian (16th century); imperial policy promotes some gods and suppresses others, and Ming edicts outlaw the martial sects.

Temples are destroyed in the Taiping and Boxer rebellions, and in 1898 Kang Youwei has temples confiscated for schools, an order soon reversed; by 1899 there are 400 Chinese temples on the American West Coast.

After 1911 modernisers condemn 'feudal superstition' and turn temples to other uses; Communist campaigns and the Cultural Revolution (1966-1976) try to destroy the religion, which revives after 1978 and is preserved in Taiwan.

Surveys find hundreds of millions worshipping gods and ancestors in China; under Xi Jinping temples may register as folk belief sites, and the religion lives on in Taiwan and among the overseas Chinese.

Under Crusader rule (1099–1291) the Druze of the Gharb and the Chouf hold Beirut and the coast for the rulers of Damascus; the Ma'an family rises after the middle of the 12th century.
The Druze chiefs of the Gharb serve the Mamluk sultans in ending what remains of Crusader rule on the coast.
After Ibn Taymiyya's fatwa, the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad defeats the Druze at Keserwan (1305) and destroys Druze sanctuaries.
Under the Ottomans the Ma'ans are the feudal lords of southern Lebanon; an Ottoman expedition attacks the Druze at Saoufar (1585).
Under Fakhr-al-Din II Druze dominion reaches from the Antioch plain to Safad, until the sultan has him killed (1635); Druze begin to move to the Hauran (1685).
After the battle of Ain Dara (1711) many Druze leave Mount Lebanon for the Hauran, and Maronites become the dominant group in Mount Lebanon.
The civil conflict of 1860 ends in autonomy for Mount Lebanon; the Hauran becomes the headquarters of Druze power.
The Druze lead the Syrian Revolution of 1925–27; Israel recognises them as a distinct community (1957), and emigrants settle in Venezuela and the United States.
In the Syrian civil war the Druze are persecuted by Islamic extremists; an attack on Suwayda kills at least 258 people (2018).

column3: Sheikh Adi ibn Musafir settles at Lalish, unites the scattered Yazidi tribes and reforms their religion; after his death (1162) his nephew leads the community.
Sheikh Hasan brings the Sheikhan principality to its height and founds a Council of Holy Men; the ruler of Mosul has him killed (1246).
Yazidism is the religion of many Kurdish tribes and emirates, from Antioch to Sulaymaniyah; its lands form seven centres, each with its sacred sinjaq.
Sunni Kurdish tribes ransack Lalish (1414); many Yazidi chiefs are forcibly converted, and Yazidi power declines.
Under Ottoman rule Hussein Beg briefly governs Erbil (1534); fatwas of the Sheikh al-Islam legitimise the killing and enslavement of Yazidis (1566).
Ottoman expeditions strike the Yazidis of Shingal: in 1613 the Yazidis defeat them, but in 1640 an army storms Mount Sinjar and kills 3,060.
Ottoman campaigns against Sinjar and Sheikhan follow one another, some fifteen in the 18th century alone.
Muhammad Pasha of Rawanduz massacres the Yazidis of Sheikhan (1832); Yazidis flee to the Russian Empire, and in 1892 Lalish is turned into a madrasa.
Yazidis are killed in the Armenian genocide and flee to Transcaucasia; in the later 20th century many emigrate from Turkey to Germany.
The Islamic State captures Sinjar (2014): over 5,000 Yazidis are killed, thousands of women and girls enslaved and more than 500,000 flee.

column3: After the Taíno population is decimated, the Spanish colonists of Hispaniola import enslaved West Africans from about 1512, some of them priests of African religions.
The French Code Noir (1685) forbids the open practice of African religions; Spain cedes western Hispaniola to France (1697), and the colony of Saint-Domingue is born.

In Saint-Domingue, where the slave trade grows, African religions blend with Catholic and Masonic elements into Vodou, practised in secret at night; legend says a Vodou ritual at Bois-Caïman sparked the Revolution of 1791.
The Catholic Church leaves Haiti (1805–1860), and Vodou becomes the dominant religion of a land of small farmers, though Haiti's first presidents fear it.

The US occupation (1915–1934) stirs interest in Vodou; migrants take it to eastern Cuba and the United States, the Church-backed Operation Nettoyage destroys many temples (1941), and the 1987 constitution enshrines freedom of religion.
Vodou is officially recognised (2003); Vodouists are attacked after the 2010 earthquake, and major temples stand in Miami, New York and other US cities.
